title: A Subquadratic Algorithm for Computing the L₁-Distance Between Two Terrains
classifications: Theory of computation → Design and analysis of algorithms
abstract: We study the problem of computing the L₁-distance between two piecewise-linear bivariate functions f and g, defined over a bounded polygonal domain 𝕄 ⊂ ℝ², that is, computing the quantity ‖f-g‖₁ = ∫_𝕄 |f(x,y)-g(x,y)| dx dy. If f and g are defined by linear interpolation over triangulations 𝐓_f and 𝐓_g, respectively, of 𝕄 with a total of n triangles, we show that ‖f-g‖₁ can be computed in Õ(n^α) time, where α = max{(ω+1)/2, 8/5}, ω is the matrix multiplication exponent, and Õ notation hides factors of the form n^ε for any ε > 0. This bound holds for the currently best known value of ω, which is approximately 2.37. More generally, if the complexity of the overlay of 𝐓_f and 𝐓_g is κ, then the runtime of our algorithm is Õ(κ^{α-1}n^{2-α}).

      Abstract
We study the problem of computing the L1 -distance between two piecewise-linear bivariate functions
f and g, defined
            R      over a bounded polygonal domain M ⊂ R2 , that is, computing the quantity
∥f −g∥1 = M |f (x, y)−g(x, y)| dx dy. If f and g are defined by linear interpolation over triangulations
Tf and Tg , respectively, of M with a total of n triangles, we show that ∥f − g∥1 can be computed
in Õ(nα ) time, where α = max{(ω + 1)/2, 8/5}, ω is the matrix multiplication exponent, and Õ
notation hides factors of the form nε for any ε > 0. This bound holds for the currently best known
value of ω, which is approximately 2.37. More generally, if the complexity of the overlay of Tf and
Tg is κ, then the runtime of our algorithm is Õ(κα−1 n2−α ).

 1      Introduction
Combining tools from computational geometry and computer algebra has led to new results
that defy intuitive lower bounds. For example, using algebraic tools, it is possible to compute
the centroid of the vertices in an arrangement of n lines in the plane in O(n log2 n) operations,
without computing the Θ(n2 ) vertices [5]. One notable algebraic tool used for this problem is
an algorithm to evaluate efficiently a univariate polynomial on multiple points [13]. This tool

      was used to speed up, among others, the computation of Shapley values in the plane [10], the
      location of points among wireless transmitters [6], and the computation of the L2 -distance
      between two piecewise-linear bivariate functions f and g [16].
          Bivariate functions over a planar domain are ubiquitous in geographical information
      systems, where they are used to represent a digital elevation model of a geospatial area, or,
      more generally, a function over a two-dimensional region such as precipitation, air pollution,
      population density, or quantities of wine production. One way to represent such a function is
      to triangulate the underlying domain and define a linear function over each triangle, resulting
      in a piecewise-linear function, often referred to as a triangulated irregular network (TIN).
      In this paper, we design an efficient algorithm for computing the L1 -distance between two
      piecewise-linear bivariate functions.

      Problem statement. Let M be a bounded polygonal region of R2 , and let f, g : M → R
      be two piecewise-linear functions defined over their common domain M. Each of f, g is
      associated with a triangulation of M, denoted by Tf , Tg , respectively, and f (resp., g) is
      defined to be linear over each triangle of Tf (resp., Tg ). Note that Tf and Tg are not
      assumed to be the same. Let n be sum of the numbers of vertices in Tf and Tg . The graph
      of f (or g) is a xy-monotone polyhedral surface in R3 , referred to as a terrain. For any
      integer p > 0, we define the Lp -distance between f and g to be
                      Z                         1/p

      The goal in this paper is to compute ∥f − g∥1 .
          We will work in the Real RAM model [18], where inputs and intermediate values are real
      numbers and where algebraic operations and comparisons on real values can be performed
      in constant time, but modulus or rounding-to-an-integer operations are not allowed. We
      assume that the coefficients of the piecewise-linear functions f and g and the coordinates of
      the triangles in Tf and Tg are real numbers.

      Related work. The problem of comparing two terrains, defined over the same polygonal
      domain, has been addressed in previous work [2, 16]. Their focus was on identifying a linear
      dependence between two functions or terrains. Agarwal et al. [2] studied the problem of
      computing the minimal distance

         σp (f, g) = min∥sf + t − g∥p                                                            (2)
                      s,t


      for p = 1, ∞, minimizing over scaling factor s and translation t. They showed that σ∞ (f, g)
      can be computed in Õ(n4/3 ) time (as stated in the abstract, Õ notation hides polylogarithmic
      factors), and that an (1 + ε)-approximation of σ1 (f, g) can be computed in O(n/ε) time if
      Tf and Tg are identical. However if Tf and Tg are different, the runtime of their algorithm
      is O(κ/ε), where κ is the complexity of the overlay of the two triangulations; κ = Θ(n2 ) in
      the worst case.
          Moroz and Aronov [16] showed that even for unaligned triangulations, ∥f − g∥2 and
      σ2 (f, g) can be computed in O(n log4 n log log n) time. This bound also applies to computing
      the L2p -distance, where p is a constant positive integer. Unfortunately, these approaches
      do not extend to computing σ1 (f, g) or ∥f − g∥1 in subquadratic time in the general case.
      One notable obstacle is that the L1 -distance involves the absolute value function, which is
      not polynomial. One key algebraic tool used in [16] to expedite the computation of ∥f − g∥2
P. K. Agarwal, B. Aronov, O. Devillers, C. Knauer, and G. Moroz                                          4:3


is the evaluation of a univariate polynomial of degree n on n points in Õ(n) operations.
Fast univariate multipoint evaluation algorithms in the Real RAM model have been known
since 1972 [13]. A subquadratic multipoint-evaluation algorithm for bivariate polynomials
was not known until much later [17], and developing fast multipoint-evaluation algorithms for
multivariate polynomials is still an active research area [19]. We note that, if the coefficients
of polynomials as well as coordinates of points are integers or in finite fields, then algorithms
for multipoint evaluation are known to be near-linear in the size of the output [9, 14].

Our results. The main result of the paper is a subquadratic algorithm for computing
∥f − g∥1 . Its runtime depends on ω, the standard matrix multiplication exponent, which is
known to be less than 2.371552 [20] and conjectured by some to be 2.

▶ Theorem 1. Let f and g be two bivariate functions defined by linear interpolation over
triangulations Tf and Tg , respectively, over a common bounded domain M with a total of n
triangles, then ∥f − g∥1 can be computed in Õ(nα ) time, where α = max{(ω + 1)/2, 8/5} and
O(nω ) is the time required to multiply two n × n matrices; currently the best known value of
ω is around 2.37. If the complexity of the overlay of Tf and Tg is κ, then ∥f − g∥1 can be
computed in Õ(κα−1 n2−α ) time.

    This result is based on three main ideas: we first show that the problem can be reduced
to computing a double sum of rational functions, where the denominators depend only on
two variables of the outer sum (Section 2). Those sums are defined over pairs of geometric
objects that satisfy some specific algebraic inequalities. Next, we use geometric cuttings to
obtain a sign-invariant biclique decomposition of those pairs of geometric objects (Section 3).
Finally, we employ fast multipoint polynomial evaluation to evaluate those sums efficiently
(Section 4).
    Recently, we became aware of a preprint improving the bound on fast multipoint polyno-
mial evaluation [19]. This seems to strengthen the bound of Theorem 1 to O(n8/5+ε ) for any
ε > 0. We discuss this (possible) improvement at the end of the paper.


 2     Reduction to Multi-point Evaluation
In this section, we first express the desired quantity ∥f − g∥1 as a sum of integrals associated
with vertices of the overlay of Tf and Tg (in Section 2.1) and ultimately as a double sum of
low-degree rational expressions of the parameters of f and g (in Section 2.2).
     We assume hereafter, without loss of generality, that the (x, y)-coordinate system has
been rotated so that none of the edges of Tf and Tg are parallel to the y-axis, and that M
lies strictly to the right of the y-axis. Moreover, for any two triangles T1 ∈ Tf and T2 ∈ Tg ,
if f (T1 ) and g(T2 ) are not parallel, with no loss of generality, we assume that the intersection
line of their supporting planes crosses the vertical plane x = 0.

      2.2.3       Case distinctions for the volume expression
      Our goal is to provide a formula for the volume of the polyhedron between π1 and π2 above
      the triangle ABC, as a linear combination of fractions where the denominators depend only
      on two variables from the triangulation Tf or on two variables from Tg . This will allow us
      to use fast multipoint evaluation algorithms for bivariate polynomials (see Section 4).

      are deduced by symmetry. In the following, we denote by VδA δB δC the volume between π1
      and π2 above ABC for the corresponding vector of signs.

       techniques for bivariate polynomials ([17]), based on fast modular composition and linear
       algebra ([21, Chapter 12, §12.2]). Recall that we work in the Real RAM model of computation,
       where the fastest known algorithm for achieving this runs in subquadratic time [17]. As in the
       previous section, the other terms appearing in Φ(Ef , Eg ) can be computed in an analogous
       manner. We start with a technical lemma on the fast multipoint evaluation of a batch of
       bivariate polynomials.

       ▶ Lemma 5. Given n polynomials fj (x, y) of degree n and n2 points pi ∈ R2 , it is possible
       to evaluate all the fj (pi ) in Õ(nω+1 ) arithmetic operations.

       Proof. The main idea is to reduce this question to a problem of fast multipoint evaluation

of operations linear in n, this allows us to compute, for all the points in p ∈ A,

        5    Conclusion
       A recent preprint improves the bound on multipoint evaluation for multivariate polynomials.
       It shows that we could evaluate nω−1 bivariate polynomials of degree n2 on n2 points in
       Õ(nω+1 ) operations [19, Theorem 3.8]. Compared to Lemma 5 derived from earlier work [17],
       this allows us to evaluate more polynomials with the same number of operations. In turn, that
       would improve Corollary 7, and the complexity of evaluating the sum of rational functions on
       a biclique of size n × n would become Õ(n2−1/ω ) instead of O(n(ω+1)/2 ), by summing over
       batches of n2/ω points. With the currently known bound on ω, 2 − 1/ω is approximately 1.58,
       which is below 8/5. Thus the cost of computing the biclique decomposition would become
       dominant, and the total cost of computing ∥f − g∥1 could be further improved to O(n8/5+ε ),
       for any constant ε > 0.
